title: Humanistic Burden of Sjögren's Disease: A Systematic Review of Treatment Efficacy on Health-Related Quality of Life.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Sjögren's disease (SjD) is a chronic autoantibody-driven inflammatory disorder that imposes a significant burden on afflicted patients. SjD is widely underappreciated, underdiagnosed, and undertreated. This may be partly due to the absence of advanced targeted treatments addressing the root cause of the disease. While some drugs are prescribed to help improve symptoms, many patients report inadequate relief, with disease progression and frequent organ damage. This systematic literature review (SLR) assessed the effects of treatments on patients' health-related quality of life (HRQoL). This study was supplemented by a patient focus group to gain additional insight into the humanistic burden of SjD.
METHODS: The SLR was conducted using MEDLINE and Embase (OvidSP) results between January 1, 2014, and February 2, 2026, supplemented with bibliographies, Google Scholar, disease-specific websites, and conference proceedings. Articles were screened specifically for HRQoL outcomes, including patient-reported disease-specific instruments (e.g., EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Patient-Reported Index [ESSPRI]) and other tools focusing separately on fatigue and ocular/oral dryness. A small patient focus group (N = 4) provided further perspectives on disease burden and management.
RESULTS: Fifty-three records were identified from 44 unique studies related to systemic treatments, including large case series and randomized controlled trials of traditional immunomodulatory or anti-inflammatory agents and newer biological treatments (e.g., rituximab, abatacept, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide, corticosteroids, iguratimod, dazodalibep, telitacicept). Most systemic treatments provided no meaningful improvements in fatigue or ocular/oral dryness. SjD focus group participants reported persistent, overlapping symptoms, particularly fatigue and cognitive impairment, that limit daily activities. Participants expressed dissatisfaction with current treatments and a strong desire for holistic therapies that address the root cause, improve symptoms, and prevent disease progression.
CONCLUSIONS: Systemic treatments have generally focused on disease activity parameters and have shown limited efficacy in reducing patient-reported symptoms as measured using HRQoL tools in SjD, leaving a significant unmet need for patient-centered holistic therapies.

title: Screening for Neoehrlichia mikurensis and other emerging tick-borne pathogens in Swedish patients with systemic lupus erythematosus receiving B-cell-targeted therapies.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The management of moderate to severe systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) has advanced considerably with the introduction of B-cell-targeted therapies. Several emerging tick-borne diseases (eTBDs) have gained increasing attention as causes of febrile illness with potentially serious complications in predominantly immunocompromised, B-cell-depleted individuals. Since the occurrence of eTBDs remains insufficiently studied in SLE, we aimed to determine whether such infections remain undetected among patients living in a tick-endemic region of Southeastern Sweden.
METHOD: Biobanked sera (n = 143) collected during 2015-2024 from 48 SLE patients receiving rituximab or belimumab in Region Östergötland were included. As comparators, samples from patients with quiescent disease on hydroxychloroquine treatment only (n = 50) were analysed. All samples were investigated by real-time polymerase chain reaction assays for the presence of the eTBD pathogens Neoehrlichia mikurensis, Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato, Borrelia miyamotoi, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Spiroplasma ixodetis, and Babesia spp.
RESULTS: No pathogen-specific DNA for the examined eTBDs was detected in serum samples from the included patients.
CONCLUSION: Evidence suggests that B-cell-targeted therapies may raise eTBD risk; however, none of the individuals with SLE included herein was found to be infected, despite the documented presence of these pathogens in Southeastern Sweden. Our findings contrast with those from Norwegian immunocompromised patients, but are in line with data from the Danish nationwide Rheumatological Database, including patients with arthritis receiving tumour necrosis factor inhibitors. Hypothetically, higher doses of glucocorticoids impair B-cell function and increase the risk of eTBD further. Nevertheless, routine eTBD screening of patients with SLE in Southeastern Sweden is not supported by our data.

title: Case Report: A rare case of biopsy-proven lupus nephritis complicated by Graves' disease in a 39-year-old man.
abstract: Hyperthyroidism and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are both common diseases in internal medicine. Among them, Graves' disease (GD) is the most frequent cause of hyperthyroidism, while lupus nephritis (LN) represents one of the most severe organ manifestations of SLE. Basic research suggests that GD and SLE may share overlapping genetic and immunological pathways; however, whether these shared mechanisms contribute to their clinical coexistence remains uncertain. Clinical studies or case reports on their coexistence are currently limited, and we cannot effectively manage cases of co-occurrence based on authoritative guidelines or expert consensus. In this study, we report a 39-year-old male patient with biopsy-proven ISN/RPS Class IV + V LN concomitant with GD. The patient was treated with a combination of glucocorticoids, mycophenolate mofetil, and hydroxychloroquine for LN, along with methimazole for GD, supplemented by symptomatic therapy including antihypertensive and heart rate controlling agents, etc. The patient demonstrated early clinical and laboratory improvement during follow-up, although the limited follow-up precluded assessment of an established renal response.

title: Case Report: Shifting the paradigm in refractory in-stent restenosis: systemic immunomodulation with hydroxychloroquine and sirolimus.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recurrent in-stent restenosis (ISR) refractory to repeated percutaneous interventions remains a formidable clinical challenge. Despite the established efficacy of drug-coated balloons (DCBs) and drug-eluting stents, a subset of patients experience relentless restenosis, highlighting the need for novel systemic strategies targeting underlying pathophysiological drivers.
OBJECTIVES: To describe a case of extreme, refractory recurrent ISR that failed multiple DCB interventions but was associated with a marked response to systemic therapy with Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) and Sirolimus, and to discuss the mechanistic rationale and potential clinical implications.
METHODS: A 56-year-old female presented with rapidly recurring ISR in both the left anterior descending (LAD) and right coronary arteries (RCA). Over a 6-year period, she underwent 11 interventional procedures at our center and at outside institutions. Sequential trials of oral anti-inflammatory agents failed to halt the restenosis cycle. In May 2023, HCQ was initiated, and Sirolimus was added in October 2023. Serial angiographic and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) follow-up were performed.
RESULTS: Prior to systemic therapy, restenosis occurred every 6 months in both vessels. After initiating HCQ and Sirolimus, the RCA remained free of restenosis for over one year. The LAD, while requiring additional focal DCB treatments, showed a marked reduction in restenosis burden, with disease becoming highly localized. IVUS revealed neointimal hyperplasia with superimposed lipid-rich and fibrous plaques, without evidence of stent fracture or malapposition.
CONCLUSIONS: In a patient with recurrent ISR, targeted systemic immunomodulation with HCQ and Sirolimus was associated with sustained vessel patency and reduced restenosis burden. This case provides a hypothesis-generating observation that addressing systemic inflammatory and proliferative drivers may repersent a potential salvage strategy for refractory recurrent ISR, warranting further prospective investigation.

title: Case Report: Probable hepatosplenic tuberculosis mimicking undifferentiated connective tissue disease and malignancy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hepatosplenic tuberculosis is a rare form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis with nonspecific manifestations, often leading to misdiagnosis. Tuberculosis can mimic connective tissue disease by presenting with systemic symptoms and positive autoantibodies, posing a diagnostic challenge.
CASE PRESENTATION: We report a 69-year-old woman with polyarthralgia, oral ulcers, and positive autoantibodies including antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-keratin antibody (AKA), and antiphospholipid antibodies, who was initially diagnosed with undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD). Despite hydroxychloroquine treatment, she developed fever, weight loss, and neuropathy. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) revealed multiple hypermetabolic hepatic and splenic lesions and abdominal lymphadenopathy, suspicious for malignancy. Liver biopsy demonstrated necrotizing epithelioid granulomas, which were highly suggestive of tuberculosis. In the context of a positive interferon-γ release assay, compatible imaging, consideration of relevant alternatives, and subsequent treatment response, probable hepatosplenic tuberculosis was considered the most likely diagnosis. Anti-tuberculosis therapy led to significant clinical and radiological improvement as assessed at six weeks.
CONCLUSIONS: Our case highlights that probable hepatosplenic tuberculosis can mimic autoimmune diseases and malignancies. Biopsy is key to diagnosis, and treatment response may be supportive even when microbiology is negative.
